l: Colonel Openshaw, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS

K., burned papers from a brass box, made a will, and died seven weeks later in a pool; his death was judged a suicide.

l: Joseph Openshaw, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS
s: Joseph Openshaw, John’s father, inherited Elias Openshaw’s estate and money. He received five orange pips from Dundee with a warning to put the papers on the sundial, ignored it, and died after falling into an unfenced chalk-pit; his death was judged accidental.

l: London, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS

l: Pondicherry, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS

s: Dundee is the postmark on the warning letter Joseph Openshaw received in January 1885. That letter contained five orange pips and instructed him to put the papers on the sundial.

l: five orange pips, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS

l: the deaths of the Openshaws, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, V. THE FIVE ORANGE PIPS

l: the blue carbuncle theft, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
s: The blue carbuncle theft is attributed by the police-court evidence to John Horner, who was working in the Countess of Morcar's dressing-room when the jewel disappeared. The recovery of the stone in a goose leads Sherlock Holmes to investigate the sequence connecting the theft to Henry Baker.

l: the adventure of the blue carbuncle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE BLUE CARBUNCLE
s: The adventure of the blue carbuncle begins as Sherlock Holmes investigates an apparently ordinary lost hat and goose. s: Henry Baker's hat was retained with the goose and returned to him by Sherlock Holmes. Baker says that a Scotch bonnet is unsuitable for his age and gravity.

Ryder mistakenly took the wrong barred-tail goose, allowing the stone to reach the market and eventually Holmes. Holmes frightens Ryder into confessing but releases him, believing this may save him from becoming a habitual criminal and will cause the prosecution of Horner to collapse.

l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes through London, observes the inquiries at the Alpha Inn and Covent Garden Market, and helps Holmes with the fainting James Ryder. He hears Ryder’s confession and Holmes’s decision to release him.

l: Henry Baker, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: Henry Baker is identified as a member of the Alpha Inn’s goose club. Sherlock Holmes concludes that he knows nothing about the theft and traces his goose through the club’s supply chain.

l: James Ryder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: James Ryder, initially using the name John Robinson, is revealed to be the head attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. He stole the Countess of Morcar’s blue carbuncle, placed it in a goose, mistakenly took another barred-tail goose, and confessed after Holmes confronted him. Holmes releases him after Ryder pleads for mercy.

l: the Countess of Morcar, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: The Countess of Morcar owned the blue carbuncle that was stolen in the jewel robbery.

s: Mrs. Oakshott, of 117 Brixton Road, supplied twenty-four geese to Mr. Breckinridge on December 22nd. She kept and fattened poultry for the market and had two white geese with barred tails that she could not distinguish.

l: the police, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: The police arrested Horner for the jewel robbery, while Holmes believes their investigation missed the line of inquiry provided by the goose. Ryder feared that the police would search him and discover the blue carbuncle.

l: the Alpha Inn, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: The Alpha Inn is a small public-house in Bloomsbury whose landlord bought two dozen geese from Mr. Breckinridge. Its goose club included Henry Baker, and its landlord identifies Breckinridge as the supplier.

l: the Hotel Cosmopolitan, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: The Hotel Cosmopolitan employed James Ryder as a head attendant. The blue carbuncle was stolen there from the Countess of Morcar’s jewel-case.

l: Baker Street, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: Baker Street is where Sherlock Holmes, Dr. John Watson, and James Ryder return to discuss the goose and the stolen stone. Holmes displays the blue carbuncle there and obtains Ryder’s confession.

l: Covent Garden Market, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: Covent Garden Market contains Mr. Breckinridge’s stall, where the geese from Mrs. Oakshott were sold. Holmes uses the stall’s records to trace the birds and encounters James Ryder there.

l: Brixton Road, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: Brixton Road is the location of Mrs. Oakshott’s house and poultry business. James Ryder went there after the theft and hid the blue carbuncle inside a goose.

l: the goose club, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: The goose club at the Alpha Inn supplied Henry Baker with a goose. Its birds form the first link in Holmes’s investigation into the stolen blue carbuncle.

l: the geese, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door

l: the blue carbuncle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: The blue carbuncle was stolen from the Countess of Morcar and hidden by James Ryder inside a goose. The goose carrying it reached Holmes, who keeps the stone in his strong-box and displays it to Ryder.

l: Mrs. Oakshott’s poultry business, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: Mrs. Oakshott’s poultry business fattened geese for the market. It supplied twenty-four geese to Mr. Breckinridge, including the goose that carried the blue carbuncle.

l: the jewel robbery, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: The jewel robbery involved the theft of the Countess of Morcar’s blue carbuncle from the Hotel Cosmopolitan. James Ryder and Catherine Cusack arranged circumstances that caused suspicion to fall on Horner.

l: the police-court proceedings against John Horner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: Horner was arrested and placed in the dock for a crime of which Holmes says he knew nothing. Holmes concludes that the case must collapse because Ryder will not appear against Horner.

l: the blue carbuncle theft, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: Ryder’s theft was the deliberate stealing of the Countess of Morcar’s blue carbuncle after he and Catherine Cusack helped implicate Horner. Ryder hid the stone in a goose but never recovered it because he took the wrong bird.

l: the adventure of the blue carbuncle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: The blue carbuncle investigation follows the stone through Henry Baker’s goose, the Alpha Inn, Mr. Breckinridge, and Mrs. Oakshott’s poultry business. Holmes solves the investigation by identifying Ryder and securing his confession.

l: the Alpha Inn’s goose supply chain, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “So much for Mr. Henry Baker,” said Holmes when he had closed the door
s: The Alpha Inn’s goose supply chain runs from Mrs. Oakshott at Brixton Road to Mr. Breckinridge at Covent Garden Market, then to Mr. Windigate of the Alpha Inn and its goose club. Holmes reconstructs this chain to locate the goose that carried the blue carbuncle.

l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: Helen Stoner visits Sherlock Holmes at Baker Street in terror, seeking help regarding the suspicious death of her sister Julia and a recent low whistle heard in Julia's former bedroom. She explains the violent history of her stepfather, Dr. Grimesby Roylott, and describes Julia's death after she cried out about a “speckled band.” Helen is now engaged to Percy Armitage, but fears that the same danger threatens her after moving into Julia's room. Holmes discovers five-finger bruises on Helen's wrist and decides to travel with Dr. Watson to Stoke Moran to investigate.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: Sherlock Holmes receives Helen Stoner at Baker Street and questions her closely about her sister's death, the whistle, the bedroom, and the circumstances at Stoke Moran. He identifies mud and a return ticket as evidence of Helen's journey, notices five livid finger marks on her wrist, accuses her of screening her stepfather, and agrees to investigate the manor with Dr. Watson.

l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: Dr. Watson is awakened by Sherlock Holmes and accompanies him to hear Helen Stoner's account. He agrees to travel with Holmes to Stoke Moran and inspect the rooms.

l: Helen Stoner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: Helen Stoner comes to Sherlock Holmes in a state of terror because she has heard the same low whistle that preceded her sister Julia's death after moving into Julia's former room. She describes Dr. Grimesby Roylott's violence, Julia's death, and her own impending marriage, and Holmes finds five livid finger marks on her wrist.

l: Dr. Grimesby Roylott, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: Dr. Grimesby Roylott is Helen Stoner's stepfather and the last survivor of the Roylotts of Stoke Moran. He is described as immensely strong, violently temperamental, feared by the village, hostile to others, and associated with the unexplained death of Julia, though no cause was established.

l: Julia Stoner (Helen Stoner's sister), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: Julia Stoner was Helen's twin sister and was engaged to a half-pay major of marines. She died two years before this account after hearing or encountering something connected with a low whistle, and her final words referred to a “speckled band.”

l: the Roylotts of Stoke Moran, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: The Roylotts of Stoke Moran were once among the richest families in England, but four successive dissolute heirs ruined the family fortune. Their remaining estate consists of a few acres and the heavily mortgaged ancestral house.

l: Stoke Moran, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: Stoke Moran is the old ancestral home and estate of the Roylotts, located on the western border of Surrey. Helen and Julia live there with Dr. Grimesby Roylott, and Holmes and Watson plan to visit it.

l: Percy Armitage, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: Percy Armitage, the second son of Mr. Armitage of Crane Water near Reading, is Helen Stoner's friend and intended husband. He has asked Helen to marry him, and their wedding is planned for the spring.

l: the Stoke Moran manor-house, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: The Stoke Moran manor-house is very old, and only one wing is inhabited. Its bedrooms are on the ground floor, while the sitting-rooms are in the central block.

l: the three ground-floor bedrooms, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: The three ground-floor bedrooms consist of Dr. Roylott's room, Julia's room, and Helen's room, arranged along the same corridor with no communication between them. Their windows open onto the lawn.

l: the corridor, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: The corridor connects the three ground-floor bedrooms and contains a lamp. Helen entered it after hearing Julia scream and saw Julia emerge from her room.

l: the gipsies, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: The gipsies are allowed by Dr. Grimesby Roylott to camp on the bramble-covered land at Stoke Moran. Helen initially suggested that they might have caused or explained the low whistle, and Julia's reference to a “speckled band” was possibly connected in Helen's mind with their spotted head handkerchiefs.

l: the cheetah, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: The cheetah is one of the Indian animals kept by Dr. Grimesby Roylott and allowed to wander freely over the grounds. Its presence contributes to Helen and Julia's practice of locking their bedroom doors at night.

l: the baboon, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: The baboon is one of the Indian animals kept by Dr. Grimesby Roylott and allowed to wander freely over the grounds. Its presence contributes to the sisters' feeling that they were not safe unless their bedroom doors were locked.

l: the low whistle, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: The low whistle was heard by Julia at about three in the morning during the nights before her death. Helen heard a similar whistle immediately after Julia screamed and again two years later when Helen slept in Julia's former room.

l: the metallic sound, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: Helen says that after hearing the low whistle on the night of Julia's death, she heard a clanging or metallic sound like a mass of metal falling. Holmes questions whether she is certain of this sound, since the storm and the old house may have confused her.

l: the speckled band, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: The “speckled band” was Julia Stoner's final intelligible reference as she lay dying. Helen is uncertain whether it referred to a group of people, such as the gipsies, or was merely delirious speech.

l: Julia Stoner's death, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: Julia Stoner's death occurred two years before Helen consulted Holmes, shortly before Julia's wedding. She was found convulsed and unconscious after crying out, and medical aid failed; the coroner found no satisfactory cause, no poison, no violence, and no way for an intruder to have entered her locked room.

l: Helen Stoner's impending marriage, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: Helen Stoner is engaged to Percy Armitage and expects to marry in the spring. She says her stepfather has offered no opposition, but her move into Julia's former room and the repeated whistle have caused her to fear for her safety.

l: the locked bedroom, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: The sisters customarily locked their bedroom doors at night because of the cheetah and baboon. On the night of Julia's death, her door was secured from the inside, while the barred windows, solid walls, and blocked chimney appeared to exclude any intruder.

l: the five-finger bruises, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: The five-finger bruises are livid marks on Helen Stoner's wrist, showing the impressions of four fingers and a thumb. Sherlock Holmes uses them to establish that Helen has been cruelly handled, although Helen excuses Dr. Roylott by saying he may not know his own strength.

l: fear and nervous shock, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, VIII. THE ADVENTURE OF THE SPECKLED BAND
s: Helen believes that Julia died from pure fear and nervous shock because no poison, violence, or other cause was found. Her own terror is intensified by hearing the low whistle in Julia's former room, but the text does not establish that this belief is correct.

l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
s: Sherlock Holmes and Watson investigate the suspicious death of Helen Stoner’s sister and the danger facing Helen at Stoke Moran. Dr. Grimesby Roylott confronts Holmes, threatens him, and demonstrates his strength by bending a poker. Holmes examines Stoke Moran mansion, discovers a dummy bell-rope, a useless ventilator, a saucer of milk, and a tied dog lash, and concludes that Roylott has strong financial motives to prevent his stepdaughters’ marriages. Holmes instructs Helen to leave a signal and spend the night in another room while he and Watson investigate the danger.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
s: Sherlock Holmes considers the nocturnal whistles, the gipsies, Dr. Grimesby Roylott’s financial interest, the dying woman’s words, and the metallic clang as possible clues. He confronts Roylott’s threats calmly, investigates the will of the deceased wife, examines Stoke Moran mansion, and concludes that Helen Stoner’s life may be in danger. He orders Helen to signal him after Roylott retires so that he and Watson can investigate her room during the night.

l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
s: John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Stoke Moran mansion, observes Roylott’s confrontation, and assists in examining the rooms and grounds. He carries a revolver at Holmes’s request and joins Holmes in planning to spend the night investigating the danger threatening Helen Stoner.

l: Dr. Grimesby Roylott, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
s: Dr. Grimesby Roylott visits Holmes after tracing Helen Stoner to him and demands to know what she has said. He threatens Holmes, bends a steel poker with his hands, and leaves after warning Holmes not to meddle in his affairs. Holmes learns from the will that Roylott has a strong financial motive for preventing his stepdaughters’ marriages.

l: Helen Stoner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
s: Helen Stoner meets Holmes and Watson at Stoke Moran after Roylott has gone to town. She confirms details about the rooms, shutters, bell-rope, ventilator, and repairs, and agrees to follow Holmes’s instructions by signaling from her window and sleeping in another room. Holmes warns her that her life may depend on obeying him.

l: Julia Stoner (Helen Stoner's sister), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
s: Julia Stoner is identified as Helen Stoner’s sister, who died mysteriously in the middle bedroom at Stoke Moran. The examination of the room reveals features that Holmes considers connected with her death.

l: the gipsies, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
s: The gipsies are connected with Dr. Grimesby Roylott and are on intimate terms with him. Holmes considers their presence, the nocturnal whistles, and the dying woman’s reference to a band as possible elements of the mystery, but he cannot determine what they did.

l: Stoke Moran, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, “And what do you think of it all, Watson?” asked Sherlock Holmes,
s: Stoke Moran is the place where Dr. Grimesby Roylott lives and where Helen Stoner’s sister died. Holmes and Watson travel there to investigate the circumstances surrounding the death and the danger facing Helen.
